findings.title: SOQL injection in searchAccounts method
findings.explanation: The searchKey parameter is directly concatenated into the SOQL query string without sanitization. An attacker can inject malicious SOQL to access unauthorized data or bypass query limits.
findings.remediation: Use a bind variable instead: 'String searchPattern = '%' + String.escapeSingleQuotes(searchKey) + '%'; String query = 'SELECT Id, Name, Industry FROM Account WHERE Name LIKE :searchPattern LIMIT 50';' or use static SOQL with a bind variable directly.

findings.title: Missing FLS enforcement on returned Opportunity fields
findings.explanation: The method queries Opportunity.Amount with USER_MODE and returns the entire Opportunity object to the client. While USER_MODE enforces CRUD and sharing on the query, it does not strip inaccessible fields from the returned sObject. A user without read access to Amount could still see it in the Lightning component response.
findings.remediation: Use Security.stripInaccessible(AccessType.READABLE, new List<Opportunity>{opp}) before returning the record, or construct a wrapper class that only exposes Id, Name, and StageName to ensure field-level security is fully enforced on the response.

findings.title: Insufficient input validation on stageName parameter
findings.explanation: The stageName parameter is accepted from the client without validation against valid Opportunity stage values. While Salesforce will reject invalid picklist values on DML, a malicious user could attempt to set stages they should not (e.g., skipping required stages, moving backwards in the sales process), bypassing business logic or approval processes.
findings.remediation: Validate the stageName against an allow-list of permitted stage transitions based on the current stage and user role. Use Schema.DescribeFieldResult to retrieve valid picklist values and implement business rules to ensure only appropriate stage progressions are allowed.

findings.title: FLS violation on Contact.Birthdate field
findings.explanation: The SOQL query retrieves Contact.Birthdate and returns it in the Contact object, but the permission set explicitly denies read access to this field (readable=false). Apex runs in system mode and ignores FLS by default, exposing sensitive birthdate data to users who should not see it.
findings.remediation: Remove Birthdate from the SELECT clause, use WITH USER_MODE in the SOQL query, or apply Security.stripInaccessible(AccessType.READABLE, contacts) before returning the Contact to enforce field-level security and respect the permission set configuration.

findings.title: FLS violation on Contact.Email field
findings.explanation: The SOQL query retrieves Contact.Email and returns it in the Contact object, but the permission set does not grant any access to the Email field. Users with only this permission set should not be able to read Email data, yet the Apex code exposes it because FLS is not enforced.
findings.remediation: Remove Email from the SELECT clause, use WITH USER_MODE in the SOQL query, or apply Security.stripInaccessible(AccessType.READABLE, contacts) before returning to ensure only fields the user has permission to read are exposed.

findings.title: without sharing bypasses record-level security on Cases
findings.explanation: The class is declared 'without sharing' and is @AuraEnabled, meaning it ignores record-level sharing rules. Users can retrieve all Cases in the org (up to 200) regardless of ownership or sharing settings, potentially exposing sensitive case data belonging to other customers or accounts.
findings.remediation: Change the class declaration to 'public with sharing class CaseHistoryController' to enforce record-level sharing rules and ensure users only see Cases they have access to through sharing rules, ownership, or role hierarchy.

findings.title: Excessive system permissions granted to support agents
findings.explanation: The permission set grants ModifyAllData, ViewAllData, and AuthorApex to tier-1 support agents whose stated purpose is only to view and close cases. These are administrator-level permissions that allow unrestricted access to all data across the org and the ability to write and deploy code.
findings.remediation: Remove ModifyAllData, ViewAllData, and AuthorApex permissions. Grant only the specific object and field permissions needed for case management. The existing Case object permissions (allowRead and allowEdit) are sufficient for the stated purpose.

findings.title: Unnecessary API access for support agents
findings.explanation: The permission set grants API access to support agents whose role is to close cases through the UI. API access allows programmatic access to Salesforce data and can be used to bypass UI controls or extract data in bulk.
findings.remediation: Remove the ApiEnabled permission unless support agents have a documented business need to access Salesforce through external integrations or API tools. For standard case management through the Salesforce UI, API access is not required.

findings.title: Guest user can access Contact data without sharing enforcement
findings.explanation: The class is declared 'without sharing' and is exposed to unauthenticated guest users via the Partner Site Profile. Guest users can call findContacts to retrieve any Contact record by last name, bypassing record-level sharing rules and potentially exposing sensitive contact information (email, phone) that should not be public.
findings.remediation: Change the class declaration to 'with sharing' to enforce record-level security. Additionally, add WITH USER_MODE to the SOQL query or use Security.stripInaccessible to enforce field-level security. Validate that only public-safe Contact records are returned, potentially by filtering on a 'Public' flag or using a sharing rule to limit guest user access.
